sample_unit: participants (Cookie Theft picture description transcripts from DementiaBank)

links.outcome: LLM scoring error versus three-human-rater consensus on Cookie Theft content units
links.effect: No significant differences in MAE between best-performing models and human raters; LLMs showed significantly higher interrater reliability than human raters.
links.quote: LLMs demonstrated comparable accuracy to human raters in scoring the Cookie Theft task, with no significant differences in mean absolute error (MAE) between the best performing models and human raters.

links.outcome: Reproducibility of LLM scoring across repeated runs/prompt strategies (self-consistency, reliability)
links.effect: LLMs showed significantly higher interrater reliability than human raters; Claude 3 Opus and GPT-4o had highest accuracy and reliability; self-consistency showed limited benefits.
links.quote: Notably, LLMs showed significantly higher interrater reliability compared to human raters.

unlisted_practices: Few-shot prompting to improve LLM scoring accuracy

screen.reason: The study empirically evaluates LLMs on scoring a neuropsychological assessment (Cookie Theft task) and explicitly compares the impact of deployment/prompting techniques including few-shot learning, prompt chaining, and self-consistency.

primary.practice: prompting strategies (few-shot learning, prompt chaining, self-consistency)
